chapters.title: Chapter 1: What a Trade War Actually Is

lessons.title: The 2018-19 US-China Trade War: A Case Study in How These Things Unfold

children.text: The US-China trade war of 2018-19 is the reference case every later trade war gets compared to, including the US tariffs on India you saw in the last lesson. It ran for roughly two years, moved through several escalating rounds, pulled in currency policy once tariffs stopped being enough, and ended in a deal that was never fully honored. If you understand its shape, you understand the template.

events.title: Section 232 Tariffs Announced
events.description: The US imposes a 25% tariff on steel and 10% on aluminum imports from most countries, citing national security. This applies globally, not just to China, but sets the tone.

events.title: China's First Retaliation
events.description: China announces tariffs on 128 US products, including pork and fruit, in response to the steel and aluminum tariffs. The US separately proposes its first China-specific tariff list.

events.title: The Trade War Officially Begins
events.description: The US imposes 25% Section 301 tariffs on $34 billion of Chinese goods. China retaliates within hours on an equal value of US goods, mostly agriculture.

events.title: Round Three: $200 Billion
events.description: The US adds a 10% tariff on $200 billion of Chinese imports. China retaliates on $60 billion of US goods.

events.title: Talks Collapse, Tariffs Double
events.description: Negotiations break down. The US raises the September round's tariff from 10% to 25%. China retaliates further.

events.title: The Yuan Breaks 7
events.description: China lets the yuan slide past 7 per US dollar for the first time since the 2008 financial crisis. The US Treasury labels China a currency manipulator days later.

events.title: Phase One Deal Signed
events.description: Both sides sign a truce. The US cancels a planned tariff round and halves another. China commits to a two-year target for additional purchases of US goods and services, a target it ultimately falls well short of, disrupted in part by the COVID-19 pandemic.

markDefs.definition: A US trade law provision allowing tariffs on imports that are judged to threaten national security, regardless of which country they come from.
A US trade law provision allowing tariffs against a specific country found to engage in unfair trade practices, such as forced technology transfer or intellectual property theft.

children.text: India was not a direct party to this trade war, but it felt three transmission channels at once. Global risk sentiment turned defensive each time tariffs escalated, and Foreign Institutional Investors trimmed emerging-market exposure, India included. Crude oil, which India imports in bulk, moved on the same global growth fears the trade war was feeding. And the rupee weakened through much of 2018, crossing 74 to the dollar in October, an all-time low at the time, as capital outflows and a costlier oil import bill hit at the same time.

body.text: Indian markets fell sharply in September-October 2018, but the trade war was only one of several forces at work that quarter. The IL&FS default (September 2018) triggered a broader NBFC liquidity crisis, and Brent crude briefly traded near $85 a barrel, both hitting Indian markets independently of anything happening between Washington and Beijing. Treat 2018's Nifty and rupee moves as a period of overlapping shocks, not a clean read on trade war impact alone.

children.text: The trade war also revived the idea of "China plus one": global buyers diversifying manufacturing away from a China-only supply chain. It became a genuine theme for Asian exporters, but India's own gains from this specific 2018-19 window were modest. Land acquisition delays and labor law friction slowed factory relocation into India during this period; the bigger push into Indian electronics manufacturing came later, through Production Linked Incentive schemes launched in 2020-21, not as a direct result of these tariff rounds.

body.title: Signs a Trade War Is De-escalating
steps: Both sides pause or cancel a previously announced tariff round
A signed agreement with specific, measurable commitments appears, not just a verbal truce
A previously weaponized currency stops being mentioned in official statements
Markets that had been pricing in escalation, equities, currency, and bond yields, start recovering before the deal is even finalized

body.title: Know the Date
body.textWithBlank: China's Phase One trade deal with the US was signed on January ___, 2020.
body.explanation: The Phase One deal was signed on January 15, 2020, roughly nineteen months after the first Section 301 tariffs took effect in July 2018.

body.text: The 2018-19 US-China trade war shows the full arc: tariffs escalate faster than either side plans for, currency becomes a weapon once tariffs stop moving the needle, and even a signed truce does not guarantee the committed numbers are ever delivered.

points: The trade war ran on two legal tracks: Section 232 (national security, applied globally) for steel and aluminum, and Section 301 (unfair trade practices, China-specific) for nearly everything else.
Tariffs escalated in rounds from July 2018 to September 2019, eventually covering the large majority of goods traded between the two countries.
China let the yuan slide past 7 per dollar in August 2019, turning currency into an active tool once tariff retaliation reached its limits.
The Phase One deal (January 2020) reduced some tariffs and set a purchase target that China ultimately did not meet, disrupted in part by COVID-19.
India felt the spillover through FII flows, crude oil prices, and rupee weakness, but 2018's market stress had multiple overlapping causes, not trade war alone.
